analysis.one_liner: Requires car makers to share the diagnostic and repair information independent shops need to fix modern vehicles.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 118 cosponsors from both parties but never got a hearing or a vote, dying in a House subcommittee.
analysis.plain_summary: Cars increasingly rely on computers, and manufacturers were restricting access to the codes and information needed to diagnose and repair them. This bill would have required automakers to disclose that information to vehicle owners and independent repair shops, with the Federal Trade Commission writing the rules and enforcing compliance. Noncompliance would have counted as an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act, and owners or repair shops could sue in federal court.
analysis.who_benefits: Vehicle owners, who could choose any repair shop and aftermarket parts instead of being steered to dealer service departments; independent repair shops and the auto parts aftermarket, which would get access to the diagnostic information dealers have; and the more than 5 million workers the bill's findings say the aftermarket employs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Car owners and independent repair shops

how_it_helps.text: Requires manufacturers to promptly provide vehicle owners and repair facilities all information needed to diagnose, service, or repair a vehicle, including information used to activate, certify, or install replacement equipment.
Prevents manufacturers from withholding information they already give franchised dealers or other repair facilities, closing the loophole that lets dealers monopolize repairs.
Lets a vehicle owner or repair shop sue in federal court to stop violations and recover attorney and expert witness fees, with no minimum dollar amount or residency requirement.

The bill's findings note that access codes increasingly block timely, affordable repair of computer-controlled systems like brakes, transmissions, and pollution controls, and cite an aftermarket that supports roughly 5 million workers in 495,000 businesses with $200 billion in annual sales.

analysis.who_pays: Automakers and their franchised dealer service networks, which would lose the ability to steer repair work to dealers by restricting diagnostic information. Some manufacturers' information-technology and trade-secret compliance costs would rise, though the bill protects genuine trade secrets from public disclosure.

drawbacks.text: The FTC may not force public disclosure of genuine trade secrets, so some information could remain unavailable to shops if the manufacturer successfully claims protection.

Manufacturers argued during this era that releasing diagnostic code and system access raised safety, emissions-tampering, and intellectual-property concerns; the bill addresses this partly by shielding EPA emissions authority from conflicting FTC rules.
The private right of action plus fee-shifting could generate litigation between shops and manufacturers, a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are broad and everyday: cheaper, faster, safer repair options for anyone who owns a car. The costs fall on a concentrated industry and on manufacturers' compliance overhead, with the trade-secret carve-out and litigation risk as the main design compromises. On balance the bill was a consumer-competition measure with manageable drawbacks.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, referred to the Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to a subcommittee, and never heard from again — no markup, no floor vote, nothing before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Joe Barton introduced the Motor Vehicle Owners' Right to Repair Act of 2003 on July 15, 2003, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
Eight days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection, where it sat with no further action for the rest of the 108th Congress.

The bill attracted 118 cosponsors — 71 Democrats and 47 Republicans — a level of support that typically indicates a bill could advance, yet it never received a subcommittee markup, full committee vote, or floor vote.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Automakers and their franchised dealer service networks, which kept exclusive control of diagnostic information and the repair revenue that flows from it. Car owners continued to face restricted repair choices and dealer-dependent pricing.

for.name: Rep. Joe Barton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited original cosponsors including members of both parties.

for.name: Rep. Edolphus Towns
for.what_they_did: Joined Barton as an original cosponsor, giving the bill bipartisan leadership from the start.

for.name: 118 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, a large bipartisan show of support it never got to translate into a vote.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection and never scheduled a markup or moved it to the floor during the Congress.

against.name: Automobile manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against right-to-repair legislation of this era, arguing it threatened trade secrets, safety, and emissions security — the arguments that kept the bill from advancing.

sides.party_line_note: The 118 cosponsors split 71 Democrats and 47 Republicans, and the sponsor was a Republican, so the bill's support was genuinely bipartisan; the obstacle was the committee calendar, not a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to share diagnostic and repair information with anyone, ending the ability to reserve it for their dealer networks. Their interest in the bill ran directly against car owners' ability to choose cheaper repair options.
Dealers profit from service departments that are the only shops with full access to repair information; mandatory disclosure would end that monopoly and expose their service prices to competition.

industries.industry: Independent repair shops and the auto parts aftermarket
industries.note: These businesses would gain access to the same diagnostic information dealers have, letting them compete for repair work. The bill's findings describe the aftermarket as employing over 5 million workers.
